learn.title: More kinds of value
learn.body: Whole numbers are not enough. C has `char` for a single character, and `float` and `double` for numbers with a decimal point. Each takes a different amount of memory, measured in bytes.

learn.title: char
learn.body: A `char` holds one character, written in single quotes, like `'A'`. Double quotes mean text, single quotes mean one character. Under the hood a char is a small number: on common systems `'A'` is 65.

learn.title: A char is a number
learn.body: `%c` prints as a character, `%d` prints the number.

learn.title: float and double
learn.body: `float` and `double` hold decimals such as 3.14. `double` uses 8 bytes and keeps about 15 digits right. `float` uses 4 bytes and keeps only about 7. Use `double` unless you have a reason not to.

learn.title: Precision differs
learn.body: Both are one third, but float runs out of correct digits sooner.

learn.title: Sizes
learn.body: On common 64-bit systems an `int` is 4 bytes, a `char` is 1, a `float` is 4 and a `double` is 8. The `sizeof` operator tells you. Larger types can hold bigger numbers or more detail.

learn.title: Adding to a char
steps: 66 is the code for `'B'`, so printing with `%c` shows B

questions.prompt: Which type holds a single letter?
Which is a character, not text?
questions.explanation: Single quotes make one character. Double quotes make text.

questions.prompt: On common systems, how many bytes is an `int`? Type the number.
questions.explanation: An `int` is 4 bytes (32 bits) on common platforms.

questions.prompt: On common systems, how many bytes is a `double`? Type the number.
To store 3.14 with the most precision, use \_\_.
questions.explanation: `double` keeps about 15 correct digits, more than `float`.

questions.prompt: `char c = 'A';` then `printf("%d", c);` prints what on common systems?

questions.explanation: A `double` has twice the storage and about double the correct digits.

questions.prompt: Match each type to what it holds.
questions.explanation: Pick the type that matches the kind of value.
